Methods used to set management objectives for nutrients - ECOSTAT Questionnaire

ECOSTAT has a mandate to compare methods used by Member States to set management objectives for nutrients that are compatible with good ecological status and good environmental status.

This questionnaire aims to understand national approaches for setting and implementing management objectives for nutrients and to help Member States and collaborating countries to improve their approaches and, thereby, achieve the objectives of the Water Framework Directive (WFD) and the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD).

Overview of countries participationg in questionnaire

Twenty-six countries participated in this survey, five of which are land-locked countries reporting only for freshwater categories.

How are management objectives for nutrients derived (methods)? (Part A)

Q1. Have you set management objectives for nutrients for waters bodies that are exposed to nutrient pollution?

Figure 1. Number of countries responding, overview by water category.

Most countries have set management objectives for all water bodies exposed to nutrient pollution in the different water categories, with few countries considering only some of the nutrient polluted water bodies (DK, ES, FR, CY in lakes; FR rivers; ES, FR in transitional waters; and DE, NL in marine waters). Only FR in lakes, DK, FR in rivers, and FR, IT, CY in marine waters have not set management objectives for water bodies exposed to nutrient pollution. Results show that France (FR) does not follow a standardised national approach, varying according to water agency (but confirm this).

Q2. When setting management objectives for nutrients, is there a focus on reduction of phosphorus, nitrogen, or both or on the limiting nutrient?

Figure 2. Number of countries responding, overview by water category.

Responses reflect, to a large extent, an interplay between biogeography and local pressures. Most countries focus on reducing both nitrogen and phosphorus whatever the water category considered; those who focussed on one or the other did so because local circumstances meant that this was the most likely reason for problems. That would be, for example, the case of phosphorus reduction in lakes, adopted by nine countries (CZ, DK, IE, ES, FR, NL, AT, FI, SE), or nitrogen in lakes (NL) and rivers (FR) or in coastal (DE, IE, NL) and marine waters (NL). UWWTD, ND and WFD were all cited as regulatory drivers for these actions. Responses focussed on the consequences of nutrients on transitional water ecosystems, but there was also some acknowledgment of the role of transitional waters as conduits of nutrients to coastal and marine waters too.

The limiting nutrient approach is more commonly assumed in freshwater categories (lakes: DE, ES, IT, FI; rivers: BE, FR, IT, FI) than in marine influenced systems (transitional: FR, IT, coastal: FR). What is not clear from the response is how the limiting nutrient is determined in any given situation. Several responses referred to prevailing dogma that nitrogen and phosphorus are the nutrients most likely to be limiting (and, therefore, responsible for eutrophication when present in excess) and some (e.g. PL) indicated that targets were to achieve concentrations consistent with the good/moderate boundary. This, in turn, presumes a good quantitative understanding of causal relationships between nutrients and measures of the condition of the flora and fauna which can be difficult to obtain for transitional waters (Salas-Herrero et al., 2019). It can probably be assumed that exceeding supporting element standards for nitrogen and phosphorus is the default criterion for recognising a need for nutrient management. However, as Phillips et al. (2018) point out, there are a variety of approaches to setting nutrient standards, with different levels of precaution. No mention is made of more targeted, case specific approaches in the responses; however, this does not mean that they are not used in individual countries.

Figure 3. Number of countries responding, overview by water category.

Q4. Do you determine the maximum critical load or a load reduction target that is compatible with good status for nutrient sensitive BQEs?

Figure 4. Number of countries responding, overview by water category.

Nutrient critical loads or load reduction targets compatible with good status of nutrient sensitive BQEs are only set by half or less of the reporting countries in lakes (DK, DE, EL, LV, NL, PL, FI, SE), rivers (BE, DE, EL, FR, LV, LT, PL, FI, SE), transitional (DE, IE, EL, LV, NL, PL), coastal (DK, DE, IE, LV, NL, PL, FI, SE) and marine waters (DK, DE, EE, LV, FI, SE).

Q5. Is there a relationship between the management objectives set for nutrients and the nutrient boundaries set for ecological status?

Figure 5. Number of countries responding, overview by water category.

Most countries acknowledge that there is a relationship between the management objectives set for nutrients and the nutrient boundaries set for ecological status, and most commonly the management objective is to reach the nutrient concentration at good/moderate boundary. In some cases the management objective is slightly more ambitious and aims to reach the mid-point between the high/good and the good/moderate boundary as defined by the biological quality elements (lakes: PT, IS, rivers: FR, NL, PT, IS, transitional: EL, NL, PT, IS, coastal: NL, PT, IS).

Some countries used another approach to set their management objective (lakes: DE, EL, FR, IT, RO, TR, rivers: DE, FR, IT, RO, TR, transitional: DE, FR, IT, RO, coastal: DK, DE, FR, IT, CY, RO, marine: IT)
